summary: Presents a model for representing a communication network and its related details in the X.500 Directory. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: A way to draw a map of a network inside a big electronic phone book, so people can look it up.

questions: how to describe a network in x.500
what is a network image object
what are physical and image objects
subtitle: A scheme for describing a whole network, its machines and their interfaces as entries in the X.500 Directory.

tldr.problem: Information about the network itself (its nodes, links and who runs them) is scattered, and the network is too large and too spread across administrations to keep one central map.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines X.500 object classes for networks, nodes and network interfaces, plus separate 'image' objects that describe the same physical things from a protocol's point of view, and places them in the Directory tree.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental proposal, not an Internet standard. It leaves several attributes loosely defined and says security is not discussed.

today: RFC 1609 is an Experimental protocol memo and is not an Internet standard of any kind. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Network Map Is Needed
sections.content:
The memo argues that network management lacks an organized pool of information about the network infrastructure itself. Earlier attempts such as WHOIS and DNS each cover only one aspect. A network map should show how network elements are interconnected, their properties and functions, their names and addresses, administrative details and policy information.

With such a map, the memo expects to support configuration management, route management (finding alternate routes, checking routing tables for loops), fault management, service location, optimization, name and address mapping, and references to the people who administer a network.
sections.eli5: If you want to find a way around a town, you need a map. A network needs one too, so people can see what is connected to what and who to call when something breaks.

sections.title: Why X.500 and the Hierarchical Model
sections.content:
The map is global, changes constantly and is controlled by many administrations, so the memo says it cannot be serviced in a centralized fashion. It proposes the OSI X.500 Directory, a very large, highly distributed database arranged as a tree of entries, where each entry holds information as a set of attributes.

In the memo's model, a network is the medium for transmitting information, with zero or more network elements that each have at least one interface on it. Networks may be simple (an ethernet, a cable) or composite, made of sub-networks. A gateway with several interfaces can serve as the external gateway of several networks.
sections.eli5: No single person can draw a map of the whole world's networks, so many people each keep their own page, and the Directory ties the pages together.

sections.title: Physical Objects and Images
sections.content:
The memo defines three object classes. CommunicationObject (CO) is the parent of everything. PhysicalCommunicationObject (PCO) describes real things, with attributes such as owner and locality. ImageCommunicationObject (ICO) describes a view of a thing, called an image, and carries an imageOf attribute that points to a physical object or another image.

This lets several logical networks, such as IP, XNS, SNA and OSI, coexist on the same physical network while each is described in its own way. Every CO may have description, adminContact and technContact attributes.
sections.eli5: A school building is one real thing, but the fire plan, the class timetable and the bus route each show it differently. Images are those different pictures of the same real thing.

sections.title: Physical and Image Schemas
sections.content:
The physical classes are network, node and networkInterface. A network must have a networkName and may have attributes such as externalGateway, nwType (composite, or a line type like bus, ring, star, mesh, point-to-point), media, speed, traffic and configuration history. A node must have a nodeName and may give machineType and OS. A networkInterface must have a networkInterfaceName and may give an address and a connectedNetwork pointer.

Each physical class has an image counterpart: networkImage, nodeImage and networkInterfaceImage. The memo cannot list all image attributes because they vary by view, and recommends defining subclasses for each logical view. networkImage has, for example, an optional charge attribute that the memo says needs further definition.
sections.eli5: Each thing gets a form to fill in: a network form, a computer form and a plug form. The image forms are the same idea, but filled in from one protocol's point of view.

sections.title: Placement in the Directory Tree
sections.content:
Network information normally sits below the organization that maintains the network. One network object gives general descriptions, node objects sit below it, and networkInterface objects sit below the nodes. A network can be divided into sub-networks, which repeat the same structure, and the entries may also be kept under organizationalUnit entries with pointers from the root network. The same structure holds for the image objects.

The schema aims to avoid data duplication, preserve administrative boundaries and controls, and keep the number of pointers minimal. Caching policies are not addressed and are left to be decided locally. Security is only touched on by the belief that X.500 access control policies give a reasonably secure framework, and the Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: Each company keeps its network pages in its own drawer of the big filing cabinet, with computers filed under their network and plugs filed under their computer.
